## Cards

### 01 · Peer support is its own kind of care
Group: **Start here** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

- Ostomy Canada Society runs chapters and peer support groups across the country, searchable by distance from where you live `1.1`
- Their Visitor Program trains people who have an ostomy to talk with people who have just had one — lived experience, not clinical advice `1.2`
- If you are between roughly 20 and 40, ask about Gutsy Gang social clubs — they run in Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, and Niagara `1.3`

> **Note** `1.note` — A peer visitor is not a substitute for your NSWOC. Most people find they want both.

### 02 · What your surgery actually changed
Group: **Eating again** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

- Food is broken down in the stomach and small intestine, and that part is usually unchanged — this is why you still absorb your nutrition `2.1`
- The colon’s main job is reclaiming water and salt from what is left, and forming stool. A colostomy leaves most of that intact; an ileostomy bypasses it almost entirely `2.2`
- A urostomy does not change how food is digested. It carries urine from the kidneys out through the stoma, so it no longer reaches the bladder, and most of the food questions here are not yours. Fluid is the opposite: you need more of it than before, steadily through the day, because a well-flushed system is what protects against infection and stones. Ask your urologist or NSWOC what daily target fits you ✎ `2.3`

> **Note** `2.note` — This is the single most useful thing to understand: an ileostomy is not "a colostomy higher up". The missing colon is why output is looser, why fluid and salt matter more, and why the advice differs.

### 03 · The first few weeks
Group: **Eating again** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

- Most teams suggest a lower-fibre period straight after surgery. It is temporary, and it is about swelling at the stoma rather than about fibre being bad for you `3.1`
- Your stoma is swollen at first and shrinks over the following weeks, so the opening it can pass comfortably gets bigger too `3.2`
- Appetite is often poor early on. Small, frequent meals tend to sit better than three large ones `3.3`

> **Note** `3.note` — How long this lasts is your surgical team’s call, not a fixed rule — it varies by surgery and by person. Ask when you should be moving on rather than assuming.

### 04 · Adding foods back
Group: **Eating again** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

- One new food at a time, in a small amount, with a couple of days before the next one — otherwise you cannot tell what caused what `4.1`
- Chew far more than feels necessary. With an ileostomy especially, chewing is doing work your colon used to do `4.2`
- Keep a rough note for a few weeks. Patterns show up quickly and then you can stop writing things down `4.3`

> **Note** `4.note` — Tolerance is genuinely individual. Two people with the same surgery often land on completely different lists, so treat anyone else’s "foods to avoid" list — including one you find online — as a starting hypothesis rather than a rule.

### 05 · Foods people often find need care
Group: **Eating again** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

**Commonly reported as harder to pass** `5.s1`

- Fibrous or stringy foods — celery, corn, mushrooms, coconut, pineapple, dried fruit `5.s1.1`
- Skins, pips and casings — apple peel, sweetcorn, nuts, popcorn, sausage skins `5.s1.2`

**How to approach them rather than avoid them forever** `5.s2`

- Cut small, cook well, chew thoroughly, and try a small amount on a day when you are not out `5.s2.1`
- Plenty of people go back to all of these. The point is caution, not a permanent ban `5.s2.2`

> **Note** `5.s2.note` — If you have an ileostomy and have had a blockage before, talk to your NSWOC or a dietitian before reintroducing this group. That is a different conversation from a first attempt.

### 06 · Fluid and salt
Group: **Eating again** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- With an ileostomy you lose more water and more sodium than you did before, and you lose it steadily rather than noticeably `6.1`
- Thirst is a late signal. Darker urine, headache, cramps, and feeling flat often arrive first `6.2`
- Plain water alone can sometimes make high output worse — an oral rehydration solution replaces salt as well as fluid `6.3`

> **Note** `6.note` — Ask your NSWOC or pharmacist what to keep at home before you need it. Rehydration solutions are cheap, keep well, and are far more useful bought in advance than at 2am.

### 07 · Gas, odour and noise
Group: **Everyday effects** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Gas usually settles over the first months as your gut adapts — early gas is not a sign of how things will stay `7.1`
- Swallowed air is a bigger contributor than most people expect: eating quickly, straws, chewing gum, fizzy drinks `7.2`
- Filters wet out and stop working. That is the filter doing its job and reaching the end of it, not a defect `7.3`

### 08 · Thicker or looser output
Group: **Everyday effects** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

**Often reported as thickening** `8.s1`

- Starchy foods — white rice, pasta, bread, potato without skin, banana, smooth peanut butter, marshmallows `8.s1.1`

**Often reported as loosening** `8.s2`

- Very sugary drinks, alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, and large amounts of fruit `8.s2.1`

> **Note** `8.s2.note` — These are patterns many people notice, not instructions. If you are using food to manage persistent high output rather than an occasional day, that needs an NSWOC or dietitian rather than a longer list of foods.

### 09 · The medication question
Group: **Everyday effects** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

- Extended-release, slow-release and enteric-coated tablets are designed to dissolve over a long stretch of gut — with an ileostomy they can pass straight through, intact and unabsorbed `9.1`
- People sometimes see whole tablets in the pouch. That is worth reporting rather than ignoring `9.2`
- This can quietly affect anything that matters — blood pressure, thyroid, mental health medication, contraception `9.3`

> **Note** `9.note` — Bring your full medication list to a pharmacist and say you have an ileostomy. There is often an immediate-release or liquid alternative. Do not stop or change anything yourself.

### 10 · Flying with supplies
Group: **Getting around Canada** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

**Packing** `10.s1`

- Pack your supplies in your carry-on. CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so split them — enough in the carry-on to cover the whole journey and a delay, and a backup set in the checked bag. Never let the only set be the one in the hold `10.s1.1`
- Take roughly twice what you expect to need for the trip `10.s1.2`
- Cut your barriers to size before you leave, so they are ready if you need to change on the plane. Scissors are not the reason — in Canada, blades of 6 cm or less are allowed in carry-on. Pre-cutting simply spares you cutting a barrier on a tray table, and scissors rules are tighter in some other countries `10.s1.3`

**Security** `10.s2`

- CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so you should not be turned back for carrying them — though the final decision on any item rests with the screening officer `10.s2.1`
- Being medical supplies is not a blanket exemption from the liquids rule. That exemption covers prescription and essential non-prescription medication, and CATSA states that ostomy paste tubes must be 100 mL or less and travel in your clear 1 L bag. Treat adhesive remover, barrier spray and lubricating deodorant the same way, or pack full sizes in checked baggage `10.s2.2`
- You can ask for privacy. CATSA says you can request a private screening room, and if a physical search or a swab is needed you can ask for that to be done there. It helps to tell the officer you have an ostomy pouch, and roughly where it is, before screening starts `10.s2.3`
- Ostomy Canada publishes a printable Traveller’s Communication Card, and Coloplast Care offers a travel certificate to people enrolled in its program. Convatec’s card is written for US screening and its travel pass is a UK document, so check which version you are getting. None of these is an official pass and CATSA does not require documentation — the card simply saves explaining `10.s2.4`

> **Note** `10.s2.note` — Screening rules change and vary by country. Check CATSA’s current guidance before you fly, and note that it covers flights leaving Canada — for the return leg, check the rules where you are flying out of. What CATSA allows in your carry-on leaving Toronto is not a guarantee coming back.

**In the air** `10.s3`

- Cabin pressure falls in flight, so gas already in the pouch expands a little. In practice the effect is small and a filtered pouch vents most of it — Ostomy Canada is explicit that the pouch will not blow up `10.s3.1`
- If your pouch does balloon on a flight, the cause is usually swallowed air, fizzy drinks, gassy food, or sitting still for hours. Vent or empty it and carry on `10.s3.2`
- Empty before boarding and again during the flight rather than waiting for it to feel necessary. An aisle seat makes that discreet rather than an event `10.s3.3`

### 11 · Winter, and why things stop sticking
Group: **Getting around Canada** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Adhesive works less well when it is cold. A barrier that has been in a cold car or an unheated porch will not bond as readily `11.1`
- Warm the barrier before applying — hold it between your palms for a minute, or tuck it under your clothing against your body — then press it in place for a full minute or two. Use body heat only: not a hairdryer, radiator or microwave. Too much heat damages the adhesive, and because the stoma has no nerve endings it cannot warn you when something is too hot `11.2`
- If your wear time drops every winter, start with the temperature of your supplies rather than your skin — a barrier stored or carried cold is the more likely explanation `11.3`

> **Note** `11.note` — Store spare supplies somewhere room temperature — Ostomy Canada suggests roughly 15 to 30°C — rather than a garage, shed, or the trunk of a car. Coloplast’s instructions for use state the product must not be stored under freezing conditions. Heat is a problem too, so those same spots are worth avoiding in July as much as in January.

### 12 · Cottage, camping and going remote
Group: **Getting around Canada** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- Find out where the nearest pharmacy is and how long it would take to reach — but treat it as a backup, not a plan. Pharmacies carry a limited range and are unlikely to stock your exact barrier and pouch `12.1`
- Take at least double what you need. There is no version of this trip where running out is a minor inconvenience `12.2`
- Plan disposal, and keep the contents and the pouch separate in your head. Contents go into a toilet where there is one; in the backcountry treat them as any human waste — a cathole 15 to 20 cm deep, at least 60 m from water, trails and camp, or packed out where that is the rule. The pouch itself never goes down a toilet: it blocks the line, and a septic system or holding tank is far less forgiving than a municipal one `12.3`

> **Note** `12.note` — If you irrigate, think it through carefully before committing to somewhere without running water. A routine needs roughly 500 to 1,000 mL of lukewarm water clean enough to drink, about an hour at a toilet, and somewhere for the output to go — and it repeats every day or two. Cold water causes cramping, which is harder to manage away from a tap. If you would not drink the water, do not irrigate with it.

### 13 · Ordering across provincial lines
Group: **Practical Canada** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- Your entitlement is set by the province you live in — you qualify through your provincial coverage, not through the store. That does not mean you can buy anywhere `13.1`
- Ontario and Quebec pay a set amount and leave the choice of retailer to you. Saskatchewan will reimburse products bought in another province if you send a paid receipt showing what you purchased `13.2`
- Alberta works differently: AADL requires you to buy from an approved Alberta vendor, does not fund online-only shops, and does not reimburse people who buy on their own. In Manitoba you do not buy at all — supplies are ordered through the provincial program and shipped from Winnipeg. In British Columbia, anything ordered online has to come from a PharmaCare-authorized provider `13.3`

> **Note** `13.note` — Check your own program’s vendor rules before you order from out of province — including from us. Moving provinces is a different situation entirely and resets your coverage; that is in Funding & Coverage.

### 14 · Supplies people offer you
Group: **Practical Canada** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- Supply exchanges exist, including Facebook groups such as Ostomy Supplies Exchange Canada, and some people do find what they need this way. Ostomy Canada also advises caution: a barrier that suited someone else’s stoma, or one stored badly, can leak or damage your skin `14.1`
- Check the expiry date, that packaging is intact and unopened, and that the size matches what you use. Ask how the supplies were stored too — heat and damp shorten the life of an adhesive barrier well before its printed expiry `14.2`
- Do not accept anything whose inner packaging has been opened. Most pouches and barriers are supplied non-sterile, so the reason is less about sterility than the adhesive: once the seal is broken you cannot tell how long it has been exposed to air `14.3`

> **Note** `14.note` — Local chapters and support groups often take in surplus supplies and pass them to members who need them. Friends of Ostomates Worldwide Canada also collects surplus, but ships it to partner organizations overseas rather than to individuals here — it states it cannot support individual requests. If you are donating, it asks that items stay in their packaging.

### 15 · What coverage actually looks like in Canada
Group: **Money** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- There is no national ostomy program. The amount, the model, and who approves it all change at the provincial border `15.1`
- Moving provinces resets everything — including which forms you file and who has to sign them `15.2`
- Who signs off changes at the border: a physician or nurse practitioner in Ontario and Nova Scotia, nobody clinical in Quebec or British Columbia, and a registered nurse — usually an NSWOC — in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Saskatchewan will not accept a self-application at all `15.3`

> **Note** `15.note` — We have checked every province and territory against its own government page — see Funding & Coverage for what yours pays, who has to sign off, and the dates that catch people out.

### 16 · Programs that cost you nothing
Group: **Money** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- All three major manufacturers run free support programs — samples, phone lines, and access to ostomy nurses `16.1`
- You do not have to buy from us, or from them, to use these `16.2`
- They will also help you work out what your province covers, which is often the fastest way to get an answer `16.3`

### 17 · Awareness, on Canada’s calendar
Group: **Community** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- World Ostomy Day runs every three years, not every year — the last was 4 October 2025, and the next falls in 2028 `17.1`
- In the years between, Canada still marks the first Saturday of October, anchored by Ostomy Canada’s Step Up for Ostomy campaign `17.2`
- Chapters usually run local events — the chapter finder is the fastest way to see what is happening near you `17.3`

### 18 · Stories from people who have one
Group: **Community** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

- Reading someone describe their first month is worth more than any checklist we could write `18.1`
- We are collecting stories from Canadians with ostomies — surgery, work, travel, dating, sport, all of it `18.2`
- If you would like to share yours, tell the care team and we will be in touch about how it works `18.3`

## Referral band

**Four ways provinces pay — knowing yours saves you money** `band.heading`

- **A flat grant, paid to you** `band.1` — Ontario and Quebec send a set amount each year and you buy your own supplies. If you use more than the grant covers, the overage is yours — and may be claimable as a medical expense.
- **A percentage cost-share** `band.2` — British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Newfoundland cover a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual cap. Low income can reduce your share to nothing.
- **Supplies issued to you** `band.3` — Manitoba does not reimburse — the program sends the supplies. You are registered through an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself.
- **Only if you qualify** `band.4` — PEI is income-tiered. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick route by category — seniors, social assistance, or specific programs — so there is no general coverage to apply for.

## Resources

### Support that is already out there `res.1`
*Find your people*

These are run by patient organizations and specialist nurses, not by us. They are free, and they are better at this than any retailer.

- **Find a chapter or peer support group** — Ostomy Canada Society `res.1.1`  
  Search by distance from your postal code, from 10 km out to 500 km. Also lists Gutsy Gang social clubs for younger adults.  
  <https://www.ostomycanada.ca/find-a-chapter-peer-support-group/>
- **Visitor Program** — Ostomy Canada Society `res.1.2`  
  Trained peer visitors who have an ostomy themselves. Requested through your local chapter, usually after a referral from your surgeon or NSWOC.  
  <https://www.ostomycanada.ca/ostomy-canada-visitor-program/>
- **Find an NSWOC near you** — NSWOCC `res.1.3`  
  Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence — the clinical specialists for stoma care in Canada. Many hospitals have one; some see outpatients for life.  
  <https://www.nswoc.ca/>
- **Youth Camp** — Ostomy Canada Society `res.1.4`  
  A week at Camp Horizon in Bragg Creek, Alberta, for kids and teens with ostomies. Partial and full funding is available — ask, do not assume the fee is the barrier.  
  <https://www.ostomycanada.ca/camp/ostomy-canada-youth-camp/>

### Manufacturer support, compared plainly `res.2`
*Free programs*

All three are free and none of them require you to buy from us. We have listed what each program offers — not whose products are better, which is not our call to make. All three are run by companies that sell ostomy supplies. Read how each one uses your information before you enrol. ✎

- **Secure Start** — Hollister `res.2.1`  
  Free personalized support regardless of which brand you use, including help navigating coverage. Canadian line: 1-800-263-7421.  
  <https://www.hollister.ca/en-ca/securestartconsumer>
- **Coloplast Care** — Coloplast `res.2.2`  
  Ongoing educational support, phone access, samples, and the MyOstomy app for tracking changes and output. Consumer support: 1-866-293-6349.  
  <https://www.coloplast.ca/care-/>
- **me+** — Convatec `res.2.3`  
  Staged around the journey — before surgery, right after, and living with one. Includes video appointments with a certified ostomy nurse. 1-800-465-6302.  
  <https://www.convatec.com/en-ca/ostomy-care/me-plus-patient-support/>

### Coverage and tax help `res.3`
*Money*

Amounts and rules change, and they change by province. Always confirm against the official source before you plan around a number.

- **Provincial government programs** — Ostomy Canada Society `res.3.1`  
  The best public summary of what each province and territory covers, with links through to the official program pages.  
  <https://www.ostomycanada.ca/provincial-government-programs/>
- **Disability Tax Credit (form T2201)** — Canada Revenue Agency `res.3.2`  
  Applied for under the “eliminating” category, but having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own — the funding section walks through the test the CRA actually applies. Approval can unlock the RDSP and other credits, so it is worth reading before you start the paperwork.  
  <https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/segments/tax-credits-deductions-persons-disabilities/disability-tax-credit/eligible-dtc/eliminating.html>
- **Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB)** — Indigenous Services Canada `res.3.3`  
  Full coverage with no annual cap for registered First Nations and recognized Inuit. This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up.  
  <https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1579620079031/1579620259238>

### Guides worth downloading `res.4`
*Read more*

Written by nurses and patient organizations, free, and more thorough than anything on this page.

- **Living with an ileostomy, colostomy, or ileal conduit** — NSWOCC `res.4.1`  
  Clinician-written patient guides, one per ostomy type, including the less commonly covered ones — jejunostomy, gastrostomy, and gastro-jejunostomy. *(English and French)*  
  <https://www.nswoc.ca/guides>
- **New Ostomy Patient Guide** — United Ostomy Associations of America `res.4.2`  
  American, so the funding sections will not apply here — but the clinical and practical content is excellent and freely available.  
  <https://www.ostomy.org/new-ostomy-patient-guide/>
- **Step Up for Ostomy** — Ostomy Canada Society `res.4.3`  
  The national awareness and fundraising campaign that anchors the first Saturday of October in Canada.  
  <https://www.ostomycanada.ca/events/world-ostomy-day/>

## Pharmacist panel

- **eyebrow** `pharmacist.eyebrow` — Available in Ontario
- **heading** `pharmacist.heading` — Fit questions that do not need a waiting room
- **body** `pharmacist.body` — Product fit, restock questions, and everyday concerns — chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours (until 5 p.m. Eastern). Olivia helps with shopping anytime; she does not give medical advice.
- **cta** `pharmacist.cta` — Talk to a Pharmacist

## Closing

**Living, not managing** `closing.heading`

Most of this stops being a question within a few months. The part that does not — the money, and finding people who have one — is the part most people never find out about, which is the only reason this page needed writing. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by your NSWOC, surgeon, or physician. Fit, skin, and product choices depend on your body and your surgery — talk to your care team before changing anything. `disclaimer`
